plot_extraction.response_text:
Aboard a ship in Calcutta, the bullying first mate repeatedly targets red-haired sailor Bill Cousins. Bill and Bob Pullin disguise themselves as Hindoos so they can provoke and beat the mate ashore without being charged with mutiny. Their plan succeeds only partly: although they injure him, he gives both men a severe beating. Too proud to admit that two Hindoos defeated him, the mate returns claiming he fought off five German sailors.

Bill and Bob then discover that the carpenter’s blacking will not wash off. Fearing the mate will recognize them and punish the entire crew, their shipmates suggest desertion, but no solution is reached. When the two are summoned on deck, they claim that five foreign sailors attacked them, knocked them unconscious, and blackened their faces. The captain concludes that they were assaulted by the same supposed Germans who attacked the mate. Unable to expose the lie without admitting he was beaten by the disguised sailors, the mate remains silent. The sympathetic captain protects Bill and Bob while their coloring gradually fades, leaving the humiliated mate to vent his anger by bullying the rest of the crew.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story is a comic maritime yarn told through a framed first-person monologue. It opens with the night-watchman offering a broad, apparently philosophical observation about bullying at sea, then moves into an anecdote that illustrates—and mischievously complicates—his point. The narrative voice is that of an experienced, self-assured sailor speaking to an implied listener. His tone combines worldly wisdom, mock solemnity and selective innocence: he reports vindictive or absurd behaviour as though it were reasonable, repeatedly defending the crew’s conduct while the reader is invited to see their cowardice, self-interest and hypocrisy.

The most conspicuous stylistic feature is the sustained representation of vernacular speech. Pronunciation is rendered through eye dialect and elision—“’e,” “’is,” “ses,” “arter,” “fust,” “wot,” “agin,” “cert’nly”—while nonstandard grammar includes constructions such as “we was,” “them two men,” and “if I was them.” Maritime contractions and vocabulary, including “fo’c’s’le,” “hands,” “barque,” “mate,” “skipper,” “v’y’ge,” “holy-stone” and “turn in,” anchor the narrative in shipboard culture. The dialect is consistent enough to establish class, occupation and oral immediacy, but remains broadly intelligible. Period racial terms and stereotypes are embedded in the sailors’ speech and comic disguise plot; they function as markers of the story’s historical social attitudes rather than as neutral contemporary diction.

Dialogue dominates the story and drives both characterization and action. Exchanges are quick, adversarial and often built around literal-minded replies, insults, evasions and reversals. Characters reveal themselves less through description than through what they say under pressure. Joe Smith’s soft-spoken suggestions mask manipulation; Bill’s threats and complaints expose his volatility; the carpenter’s professional pride shades into irresponsibility; the mate’s boastfulness traps him; and the skipper’s confident deductions complete the misunderstanding. Repeated speech tags such as “ses Bill” and “ses Joe” reinforce the oral, anecdotal rhythm and keep the narration unpolished in a deliberate, performative way.

The prose alternates between short conversational volleys and longer narrative sentences linked by “and,” “but,” “then” and “well.” This paratactic syntax resembles spontaneous storytelling: events appear to be added as the speaker remembers them, with frequent transitional formulas such as “Well,” “To cut a long story short,” and “I remember.” Comic detail is accumulated through lists and escalating clauses. The attempts to remove the blacking—soap, butter, linseed oil, tea leaves and turpentine—form a particularly effective catalogue, each failed remedy increasing the farcical pressure. Descriptions are concrete, exaggerated and visual: the mate returns with his necktie around his ear, Bill and Bob resemble “two wax figgers,” and the mate swells with anger until the narrator wonders how he avoids bursting.

The humour depends chiefly on dramatic irony, reversal and escalating misunderstanding. Bill and Bob disguise themselves in order to attack the mate without punishment, only to receive a severe beating and discover that their colouring will not wash off. The mate preserves his pride by inventing five German attackers; the disguised sailors then appropriate the same lie, causing the skipper to identify a fictitious gang and to treat all three men as victims of one assault. The mate understands the truth but cannot reveal it without admitting that two supposedly “mild and meek” local men defeated him. Thus vanity becomes a mechanism of self-silencing. The final reversal is especially neat: the disguise that threatened to expose the crew becomes the evidence that protects them.

Structurally, the tale follows a clean comic arc: generalized reflection, introduction of the bully, conspiratorial plan, offstage fight, disastrous aftermath, threat of discovery, public confrontation and ironic resolution. Much of the crucial violence occurs offstage and is reconstructed through damaged bodies, conflicting accounts and boastful testimony. This keeps the emphasis on social embarrassment rather than physical brutality. Suspense arises not from uncertainty about what happened, but from whether the deception will survive contact with authority. The blacking that cannot be removed acts as both a physical comic prop and a visible countdown to exposure.

Characterization is economical and caricatural, suited to a short comic tale. Each figure has a dominant trait—the mate’s bullying pride, Bill’s resentment, Joe’s slyness, the carpenter’s complacency, the skipper’s decent but limited judgment—but these traits interact in ways that generate the plot. The crew often behaves as a collective, expressed through “we,” communal speculation, meetings and shared efforts at concealment. Yet that solidarity is opportunistic: the men encourage the attack, then suggest that Bill and Bob desert, and finally restrain them when they threaten to confess. The narrator’s insistence on the crew’s “better feelings,” “kindness” and sincerity creates a persistent gap between his moral account and their actual conduct.

The tone remains genial even when the material involves bullying, assault, threats with a razor and racial impersonation. Violence is stylized through hyperbole, slapstick and aftermath rather than treated with psychological gravity. Sentimental language is repeatedly used inappropriately—“pore black fellers,” “wictims of a cruel outrage,” “better feelings prevailed”—producing mock pathos. Understatement has a similar effect: severe beatings become “a turn with the mate” or “a doing,” and conspiracy is described as taking “a great interest” in an idea.

Overall, the style is that of a compact Edwardian comic sea story: strongly voiced, dialect-heavy, dialogue-led and built around an ingenious social trap. Its signature effect comes from the mismatch between the narrator’s complacent version of events and the reader’s clearer perception of collective guilt, vanity and absurdity. The ending restores shipboard order without delivering formal justice; instead, punishment is distributed informally, with the mate humiliated, the conspirators bruised, and the entire crew still subject to his displaced resentment.

generation.response_text:
BULLIES, said the night-watchman, folding his arms on the gate and looking over the dark river, is men wot would be very pleasant company if everybody else was twice their size. They don’t mean no ’arm, not really. It’s only their high spirits. I’ve known a man with such high spirits that it took six policemen to get ’em into a cab.

Shipboard is where a bully gets his best chance. There ain’t no street-corner to turn, and no back-door to slip out of, and if the mate says, “Come ’ere,” you’ve got to come, whether you’re busy, asleep, or dead. I knew one second mate as found fault with a hand for dying in his watch. Said it was shirking.

But pride is a useful thing in a bully. If it wasn’t for pride, I don’t know wot ordinary sailormen would do with ’em. Pride is like a rope round a man’s neck: once you get hold of the end you can lead ’im anywhere.

I remember a fust mate o’ the barque *Mary Ann*, trading out east, as was about the finest-built bully I ever see. He stood six foot two in his socks, though nobody ever see ’im in his socks except the steward, and ’e had fists like two smoked hams. His name was Mr. Grummett, and his idea of discipline was to keep everybody uncomfortable. If a man was working, he wanted to know why ’e wasn’t working faster; if a man was working fast, he wanted to know wot ’e’d been doing before.

He took a pertickler dislike to a red-’aired able seaman named Bill Cousins. Bill’s hair was the brightest thing aboard, and Mr. Grummett said it was a danger to navigation. He said a careless man might mistake Bill’s head for the port light, and he ordered ’im to keep his cap on after sunset.

Bill stood it pretty well at fust. He was a peaceable man when asleep, and even when awake he preferred talking about fighting to doing it. But Mr. Grummett was always finding little jobs for him. If there was a rusty bolt in the forepeak, Bill had to polish it. If there was a rope wanted coiling, Bill had to coil it. And if there wasn’t nothing wanted doing, the mate used to invent something and then find fault because it hadn’t been done before.

“Cousins,” he ses one morning, looking over the rail while Bill and Bob Pullin was holy-stoning the deck, “wot are you grinning at?”

“I ain’t grinning, sir,” ses Bill.

“Don’t answer me,” ses the mate.

“I didn’t know you didn’t want an answer, sir,” ses Bill.

“Are you trying to be funny?” ses the mate.

“No, sir,” ses Bill, very careful.

“Then don’t look funny,” ses the mate. “It’s agin discipline.”

Bill went on with his work, but his face got redder than his hair. Bob Pullin, wot was working alongside of ’im, told him afterwards that it was a mercy there wasn’t no gunpowder aboard.

“You’ll get into trouble one o’ these days,” ses Bob.

“I know that,” ses Bill. “The trouble’ll be about six foot two, with black whiskers.”

“Keep your temper,” ses Bob. “That’s the best thing.”

“I am keeping it,” ses Bill. “I’m saving it up.”

The mate heard the last part, and Bill spent the afternoon scraping paint in a place where there wasn’t hardly room for a rat to turn round. When he come out, Mr. Grummett asked ’im whether he’d enjoyed his rest.

It went on like that all the way to Calcutta. Sometimes the mate shoved Bill, and sometimes he knocked his cap off, and once he pulled ’im up out of his bunk at four bells because he said Bill was snoring disrespectful. Bill spoke to the skipper about it, but the skipper was a mild, elderly man and advised patience.

“Mr. Grummett has a quick manner,” he ses.

“So’s a mad dog,” ses Bill.

“There, there,” ses the skipper. “Do your duty, Cousins, and don’t answer your officers.”

“I never gets time,” ses Bill. “He answers for me.”

The skipper looked at him severe and told him to go for’ard.

By the time we got to Calcutta the whole fo’c’s’le was taking an interest in the affair. Not that we encouraged Bill to do anything wrong. Far from it. We was all steady men, with a proper respect for law and order, especially when the law was standing six foot two and could box. But we sympathized with Bill, and when a man’s shipmates sympathize with ’im, there’s no knowing wot he may be persuaded to do.

It was Joe Smith as thought of the idea. Joe was a little, soft-spoken man, with a way of looking at you as though he was sorry for your future.

He was sitting on his chest one evening, mending a sock, when the mate’s voice came down the hatch ordering Bill to go aft and wash some mud off the jolly-boat.

“That’s the third time to-day,” ses Bob Pullin.

“It’s clean now,” ses Bill.

“Then you’d better go and dirty it first,” ses Joe, biting off a thread.

Bill said several things about the mate which showed that he’d been brought up among people with large vocabularies.

“If you was to hit ’im aboard,” ses Joe, thoughtful, “it’d be mutiny.”

“I know that,” ses Bill.

“And if you hit ’im ashore,” ses Joe, “you’d get put in quod.”

“I know that too,” ses Bill.

Joe held the sock up and looked at it.

“Course,” he ses, “if ’e was to be set upon by a couple o’ strangers, that’d be different.”

Bill stared at him.

“Wot strangers?” he ses.

“Any strangers,” ses Joe. “Sailormen, for choice.”

“He’d know me,” ses Bill. “He’d know this ’air in a coal-cellar.”

Joe shook his head.

“Not if you altered yourself,” he ses.

“How?” ses Bill. “Cut my head off?”

“Black it,” ses Joe.

There was a quietness in the fo’c’s’le after that. Everybody looked at Bill’s face, and then they looked at Joe. Ginger Dick began to laugh, but stopped when Bill turned round.

“Black it?” ses Bill.

“And your ’air,” ses Joe. “You and Bob could dress up like a couple o’ natives. Loose shirts, turbans, and a bit o’ blacking. Wait for the mate somewhere quiet, give ’im a doing, and come back aboard afore he does.”

“Why me?” ses Bob Pullin, very sharp.

“You’re Bill’s friend,” ses Joe.

“I ain’t that sort of friend,” ses Bob.

“We thought you was,” ses old Ned Baker.

“There’s friendship and friendship,” ses Bob. “I’d lend ’im tobacco. I’d even lend ’im money if I was sure he couldn’t get ashore to spend it. But dressing up and fighting the mate is different.”

Bill put his hand on Bob’s shoulder.

“You’ve often said you’d like to see the mate get a hiding,” he ses.

“So I would,” ses Bob. “From a safe place.”

“You shall,” ses Bill. “Close to.”

Bob tried to argue, but there’s no arguing agin six men all telling you wot a fine, loyal character you’ve got. Besides, Joe said there wasn’t hardly no risk, and when Joe said a thing was safe it generally meant that he wasn’t going to take part in it.

The carpenter had a pot of blacking he used for marking timber and touching up odd jobs. It wasn’t ordinary boot-blacking; it was his own mixture, and he was very proud of it.

“Water won’t touch it,” he ses. “Sun won’t fade it. Salt won’t bite it. Once it’s on, it stays.”

“That’s just wot we want,” ses Joe.

The carpenter lent us the pot, though he said it was wasting good material on bad faces. Two old cotton shirts was bought ashore, and the steward provided a couple o’ cloths for turbans after we’d promised to pay for ’em at some future date. Bill wanted bracelets as well, but Joe said that would be overdoing it.

We waited till the skipper had gone to dine with an agent, and Mr. Grummett had dressed himself to go ashore. He came for’ard before leaving, just to tell us that if he found any man drunk when he got back he’d cure ’im of it in a way he wouldn’t forget.

“I don’t drink,” ses Bill, looking down.

“No,” ses the mate. “You’re foolish enough sober.”

When he’d gone, Bill’s better feelings nearly got the upper hand. He walked up and down saying that murder was hanging work, and that if Bob didn’t keep his temper there might be a serious accident.

“My temper!” ses Bob. “I’m going to see fair play, that’s all.”

“You’re going to ’elp,” ses Bill.

“I’ll ’elp you home,” ses Bob.

We got ’em dressed in the carpenter’s shop. The blacking went on beautiful. It covered Bill’s red hair until it looked like polished ebony, and when we’d finished with his face his own mother wouldn’t have known him without being told. Bob looked even better, except where the blacking had gone into one eye and made him cry.

“Stop rubbing it,” ses the carpenter. “You’ll spoil the surface.”

“I want to spoil it,” ses Bob. “It burns.”

“That shows it’s taking hold,” ses the carpenter, pleased.

Bill looked at himself in a little cracked mirror and turned his head from side to side.

“I don’t look much like a Hindoo,” he ses.

“You don’t look much like Bill Cousins,” ses Joe, “and that’s the chief thing.”

“You look like two wax figgers after a fire,” ses Ginger Dick.

Bill picked up a marline-spike, and Ginger said at once that, looking closer, he’d never seen a finer pair.

They went ashore by the accommodation ladder, keeping their heads down. One of the native boatmen called something after them, and Bob called something back. We never knew wot either of ’em said, but Bob claimed afterwards that it helped the disguise.

The plan was for them to wait near a narrow lane the mate generally used on his way back. Then, when he came along, Bill was to jostle him accidental, Bob was to jostle him from the other side, and between ’em they was to give ’im a lesson in politeness.

We stayed aboard, wondering how they was getting on. Joe said there couldn’t be no danger provided they kept cool, and the carpenter said that if either of ’em perspired too much they was to be careful not to wipe their faces on the shirts, because his blacking was expensive.

About two hours later we heard somebody coming along the wharf, singing and stopping every few yards to talk to himself. It was Mr. Grummett.

He came up the side very slow. One sleeve of his coat was missing, his collar had broke loose, and his necktie was hanging over his left ear like a pennant. His right eye was closing fast, and there was a large swelling over his jaw.

We all looked busy. Ginger Dick began coiling a rope that was already coiled, and Joe took up his sock.

The mate stood at the top of the ladder and looked at us.

“Any o’ you men been ashore?” he ses.

“No, sir,” ses Joe.

“Where’s Cousins and Pullin?”

“Below, sir, I think,” ses Joe.

The mate breathed hard.

“I’ve just had a little difficulty,” he ses.

Nobody spoke. We could see that he was waiting to be asked, but sailors has to be careful not to pry into their officers’ private affairs.

“Five of ’em,” ses the mate, after a bit. “German sailors.”

“Five, sir?” ses Joe, opening his eyes.

“Five,” ses the mate. “Big fellows. They thought they’d found an easy mark.”

“Did they, sir?” ses Ned Baker.

“They know better now,” ses the mate. “I don’t suppose two of ’em will leave their beds for a month. The others ran.”

“German sailors is very troublesome,” ses Joe.

“They chose the wrong man,” ses the mate. “One of ’em hit me from behind with a bottle. That’s how I got this.”

He touched his eye very gentle.

“And your sleeve, sir?” ses Ginger.

“Torn off while I was holding two of ’em,” ses the mate. “One under each arm.”

“Pity there wasn’t six,” ses Joe, admiring. “You could ’ave had three under each.”

The mate looked at him hard, but Joe’s face was as innocent as a baby’s. Then Mr. Grummett told us to mind our own business and went below.

We waited another hour, and then two figures came crawling along the wharf. At fust we thought they was natives looking for work; then one of ’em swore in Bill’s voice.

They got aboard somehow, and we carried ’em into the fo’c’s’le. If the mate looked bad, Bill and Bob looked worse. Bob had two black eyes, though it didn’t show much owing to the blacking, and Bill’s nose had been knocked a little out of its usual position. Their shirts was in ribbons, their turbans was gone, and they had to be put in their bunks like sacks.

“Did you do ’im?” ses Joe.

Bill opened one eye.

“Do ’im?” he ses. “There was three of us ’itting ’im together.”

“Three?” ses Joe.

“Me, Bob, and the ground,” ses Bill. “Every time we got up he knocked us down agin.”

“You must have hurt ’im,” ses the carpenter.

“Bob tore his sleeve off,” ses Bill.

“I was trying to hold on to something,” ses Bob, faintly. “He hit me for ten minutes without stopping.”

“Eight minutes,” ses Bill.

“It seemed longer,” ses Bob.

Joe told ’em that the mate had come back and claimed he’d beaten five German sailors. Bill sat up at that, groaned, and lay down agin.

“German sailors?” he ses.

“Five,” ses Joe. “Very large.”

“The liar,” ses Bill.

“You can’t call ’im a liar,” ses Joe. “Not without explaining.”

Bill thought for a moment and then smiled, though it hurt him.

“Let ’im have his five Germans,” he ses. “All I want now is to wash this muck off and turn in.”

That was where the real trouble began.

The carpenter brought a bucket of water and a lump of soap, and Bill and Bob started washing. They washed for ten minutes, and all they did was to make the blacking shine brighter. The carpenter watched with the air of a man seeing a good job properly tested.

“I told you water wouldn’t touch it,” he ses.

“Bring hotter water,” ses Bill.

We brought hotter water. Then we brought soft soap. Then yellow soap. Then the steward produced a cake of scented soap belonging to the skipper. Nothing happened, except that Bob’s face smelt like violets.

“Try butter,” ses Ned Baker.

We tried butter. After that came linseed oil, tea leaves, soda, lamp oil and a mixture of salt and vinegar recommended by Ginger Dick’s aunt for taking stains out of tablecloths.

“It ain’t a tablecloth,” ses the carpenter.

“It ain’t a face neither,” ses Bill, rubbing till his skin smarted.

At last the carpenter fetched some turpentine. That shifted a little blacking and nearly shifted Bill out of the bunk. He jumped up, yelling, and chased the carpenter twice round the fo’c’s’le with a razor. We stopped him from using it because we knew how upset he’d be afterwards.

“I thought you said it would come off,” ses Bill, when we’d got the razor away.

“I never said nothing of the kind,” ses the carpenter. “I said it stayed on. That’s why it’s good.”

“How long?” ses Bob.

“Depends,” ses the carpenter.

“On wot?”

“Wear and weather,” he ses. “Three weeks, p’raps. Six if you keeps indoors.”

There was a nasty silence.

The skipper was coming back aboard that night, and in the morning all hands would be mustered. Bill and Bob couldn’t stay hidden for three weeks, nor even three hours if the mate took it into his head to look for ’em.

“You’ve ruined us,” ses Bill to the carpenter.

“I’ve disguised you,” ses the carpenter. “That was wot you asked.”

Joe began walking up and down, thinking. We all helped by making suggestions.

“Shave their heads,” ses Ginger.

“And their faces?” ses Bill.

“Tell the skipper they’ve got fever,” ses Ned.

“Wot sort o’ fever turns a man black?” ses Bob.

“A very bad one,” ses Ned.

“You’d better desert,” ses Joe at last. “Slip ashore now and don’t come back till it wears off.”

Bill stared at him.

“And lose our pay?”

“It’s only money,” ses Joe.

“That’s easy for you to say,” ses Bill.

“Besides,” ses Bob, “we ain’t got nowhere to go.”

Joe said that India was a large country and there ought to be room for two more. Bill said he’d rather give himself up and tell the truth. That alarmed everybody.

“You can’t do that,” ses Ginger. “You’d be admitting to assaulting an officer.”

“I’ll admit your part too,” ses Bill. “The whole plan.”

“It wasn’t our plan,” ses Joe. “We only took an interest in it.”

“You blacked us,” ses Bob.

“Out of kindness,” ses the carpenter.

“You lent us the shirts,” ses Bill to the steward.

“Against my better judgment,” ses the steward.

Bill reached for the razor agin, and we had another little struggle. In the middle of it the mate’s voice came down the hatch.

“Cousins! Pullin! On deck!”

We all stopped.

“Tell ’im we’re dead,” whispers Bob.

“He’d come down to make sure,” ses Joe.

The mate called agin, louder.

Bill stood up, swaying a little, and looked round at us. His face, being black and shiny, didn’t show much expression, but his voice did.

“I’m going up,” he ses, “and I’m going to tell everything.”

He took one step, and six of us caught hold of him.

“Don’t be rash,” ses Joe.

“Think of your shipmates,” ses Ned.

“That’s just wot I am thinking of,” ses Bill.

While we was arguing, the skipper’s voice joined the mate’s. He ordered the two men on deck immediate. That settled it. We couldn’t hide ’em, and carrying ’em ashore through the porthole wasn’t practical.

Joe suddenly held up his hand.

“I’ve got it,” he ses. “You was attacked.”

“By who?” ses Bob.

“Foreign sailors,” ses Joe.

Bill stopped struggling.

“How many?” he ses.

“Five,” ses Joe.

There was a pause, and then Bill’s battered face began to brighten.

“Five Germans,” he ses.

“Exactly,” ses Joe. “They attacked the mate fust, and then they attacked you. They knocked you senseless and blacked your faces for spite.”

“Why?” ses the carpenter.

“Foreigners,” ses Joe, shrugging his shoulders. “You never know with foreigners.”

Bill and Bob looked at each other.

“It’s a weak tale,” ses Bob.

“It’s the only one we’ve got,” ses Joe.

The mate shouted for ’em a third time, and Bill took a deep breath.

“Help us up,” he ses.

We helped ’em on deck. It was a beautiful warm night, with the lights ashore shining across the water and the skipper standing by the cabin door. Mr. Grummett was alongside of him, looking even larger than usual owing to bandages.

The skipper caught sight of Bill and Bob and stepped back.

“Who are these men?” he ses.

Bill touched his forehead.

“Cousins, sir,” he ses.

“And Pullin,” ses Bob.

The skipper stared. The mate stared too, but in a different way. His mouth opened, and then shut with a snap.

“Wot’s the meaning of this?” ses the skipper.

Bill leaned against the rail.

“Attacked, sir,” he ses, very feeble. “Set upon by five foreign sailors.”

The mate made a choking noise.

“Five?” ses the skipper.

“Yes, sir,” ses Bob. “Germans.”

Mr. Grummett took one step forward, and Bill looked at him. For a moment neither spoke. The mate knew them then, and they knew he knew. But he also knew that if he said so he’d have to explain how two mild and meek-looking natives had torn off his sleeve, put his necktie round his ear, and damaged his features.

“Go on,” ses the skipper.

“We was walking peaceable,” ses Bill, “when these five Germans sprang on us. Big men they was.”

“Very big,” ses Bob.

“One of ’em had a bottle,” ses Bill.

The mate’s bandaged eye twitched.

“They knocked us senseless,” ses Bob, “and while we was unconscious they blacked us all over.”

“Outrageous!” ses the skipper.

“Yes, sir,” ses Bill. “Cruel, I call it.”

“Why should they black your faces?”

Bill hesitated.

“To insult the British flag,” ses Joe Smith from behind us.

The skipper nodded at once.

“That’s it,” he ses. “A deliberate insult. Mr. Grummett, these must be the same ruffians who attacked you.”

The mate’s face went dark red.

“Seems like it,” he ses between his teeth.

“Five German sailors,” ses the skipper. “There cannot be two gangs of five German sailors fighting British seamen on the same night.”

“No, sir,” ses Joe. “Not likely.”

“And the description agrees,” ses the skipper. “Large men, one with a bottle.”

“Exactly, sir,” ses Bill.

The mate looked as though he wanted to speak, but every time he opened his mouth Bill’s one visible eye fixed itself on him. At last he said that he supposed it might be the same men.

“Might be?” ses the skipper. “Of course it is. This is a serious matter. Three of my men attacked in one evening!”

“Three wictims, sir,” ses Joe, sorrowful.

The skipper told the steward to fetch brandy, and he made Bill and Bob drink some. Then he ordered hammocks for ’em in a cool part of the deck and said they wasn’t to do no work until they’d recovered. He even sent ashore for a doctor next morning.

The doctor looked at their faces, asked a few questions, and said he had never seen such a case. The carpenter said modestly that he hadn’t neither.

For four days Bill and Bob lay under the awning drinking beef tea and being treated like invalids. The skipper visited ’em twice a day, and every time he did, the mate had to stand by and listen to their account of the five Germans.

Bill improved it with telling. By the third day the Germans had clubs; by the fourth they had knives; and Bob said one of ’em had tried to scalp him. The skipper promised to report the matter to the authorities.

The blacking faded gradual. Bill came out patchy, with one pink ear and a red streak showing through his hair, while Bob peeled round the nose. The skipper said it was a blessing their natural colour was returning, and Mr. Grummett had to agree.

He never said a word about it. He couldn’t. That was the beauty of Joe’s idea. If the mate accused them, he accused himself; and if he told the truth, he had to change five great Germans into two ordinary sailors dressed in cotton shirts. Pride held ’im tighter than irons.

But he had to ease his feelings somehow.

So for the rest of that v’y’ge he treated Bill Cousins and Bob Pullin as though they was made of glass, while the remainder of us did nearly double work. He found rusty bolts we’d never seen before, ropes that wanted coiling six times a day, and mud on the jolly-boat when there hadn’t been rain for a week.

That’s the worst of helping a man out of a difficulty. He’s generally grateful to the wrong people.

Still, Bill and Bob got well, the mate kept his reputation, and the skipper went to his grave believing that somewhere in Calcutta there was a gang of five enormous Germans with a bottle and a pot of blacking.

And, as I said afore, pride is a useful thing in a bully—provided you don’t mind doing his share of the work.

free_generation.response_text:
On the first Tuesday of every month, the sea returned something it had taken.

At dawn, the people of Bellweather walked down to the beach carrying lanterns, baskets, and long poles. They searched the wet sand for wedding rings, anchors, silver spoons, drowned clocks, lost cargo, and once, to everyone’s astonishment, an entire piano covered in pink barnacles. No one knew why the sea kept this peculiar schedule. The oldest villagers said it had always been so. The priest said it was mercy. The harbor master said it was tides. The children said the sea simply cleaned its room once a month.

Mara Vale knew better.

The sea did not return what it had taken. It returned what it no longer wanted.

She had learned this from her father, Elias, who had vanished eleven years ago while sailing beyond the black reef. His boat came back the following month with its sail neatly folded and a single wet boot standing upright in the stern. Elias did not.

Since then, Mara had gone to the beach on every Returning Day, no matter the weather. She had been nine years old the first time. Now she was twenty, broad-shouldered from hauling nets and quiet from too much waiting.

On the first Tuesday of November, she woke before the bells.

Wind scratched branches against the roof. Rain whispered at the windows. In the kitchen, her mother sat beside an unlit stove, dressed in her gray work clothes.

“You don’t have to go,” she said.

Mara pulled on her father’s oilskin coat. The sleeves had once covered her hands. Now they stopped above her wrists.

“Yes, I do.”

Her mother looked older in darkness. “Eleven years.”

“I know.”

“If the sea meant to return him—”

“I know.”

Her mother’s mouth tightened. There had been a time when she argued. Then a time when she pleaded. Now she simply rose, lit the stove, and put a kettle on.

“Bring back driftwood,” she said. “If there is any.”

Mara nodded and stepped outside.

Bellweather sloped toward the ocean in crooked streets. Its houses were built from dark stone, their roofs weighted against the coastal wind. Lanterns bobbed ahead of Mara as villagers descended toward the shore.

At the bottom of Anchor Street, old Tomas Reed joined her. He carried a brass-hooked pole over one shoulder and wore a hat patched with sailcloth.

“Bad morning,” he said.

“Good mornings bring too many people.”

“True enough.”

They walked together through the dunes. The ocean appeared beyond them, vast and iron-colored beneath the thinning night.

The tide had retreated farther than Mara had ever seen.

Usually, Returning Day revealed a strip of black sand scattered with seaweed and debris. That morning, the water had withdrawn beyond the reef. The harbor lay empty. Boats leaned in the mud like sleeping animals. Fish flapped in shallow pools, and the black reef rose entirely from the seabed, jagged and glistening.

The villagers stopped among the dunes.

“No one goes past the harbor markers,” called Harbor Master Crenn.

He was ignored almost immediately.

Objects covered the exposed sand.

There were hundreds—perhaps thousands—stretching all the way to the reef. Chairs, bottles, knives, statues, chains, bones, lanterns, and pieces of ships from different centuries lay tangled together. A bronze cannon rested beside a child’s red wagon. Three stone saints stood shoulder-deep in mud. A forest of masts pointed toward the cloudy sky.

The people of Bellweather scattered across the seabed.

Mara descended more slowly. Something felt wrong. Returning Days were usually noisy with gulls, waves, and excited voices. Now there were no gulls. Beyond the reef, the ocean stood like a distant wall, and beneath all other sounds Mara heard a low, steady ringing.

Tomas heard it too.

“What is that?” he asked.

Mara turned her head. The sound came from somewhere east of the harbor.

They followed it past an overturned fishing boat and a row of cracked clay jars. The mud sucked at their boots. The ringing grew clearer—not a bell, exactly, but the repeated chime of metal struck by something soft.

They found a door.

It stood upright in the seabed without any wall around it, painted blue and fitted with a brass knob. A little iron bell hung above the frame. Though there was no wind, the bell swung back and forth.

Mara stared.

The blue paint was faded, but she recognized the white scratches near the bottom and the small crescent-shaped dent beside the knob. It was the front door of the house where she had been born, replaced after a winter storm when she was seven.

Tomas removed his hat. “Well.”

Mara stepped closer.

“Mara,” he warned.

She reached for the knob.

The moment her hand touched the brass, the bell stopped.

Behind her, the villagers’ shouts faded. The air smelled suddenly of bread, woodsmoke, and lavender soap. For one impossible second, Mara was a child again, standing in the hallway while her father stomped seawater from his boots.

She opened the door.

Warm yellow light filled the frame.

On the other side was not the empty seabed, but a narrow corridor wallpapered with blue flowers. At its end stood a kitchen. A kettle steamed on the stove. Someone sat at the table with his back turned.

Mara could not breathe.

The man’s hair was threaded with gray. His shoulders were thinner than she remembered, but the left one sat slightly higher, just as it always had. His hand rested beside a white cup.

“Papa?”

He turned.

Eleven years fell away from his face when he smiled.

“There you are,” Elias said.

Mara crossed the threshold.

Tomas shouted, but the door swung shut behind her.

The kitchen was exactly as it had been in childhood. Copper pans hung above the stove. A crack ran through the blue sugar bowl. Her yellow scarf dangled from a peg, though it had been lost when she was six.

Elias stood uncertainly.

Mara had imagined this moment a thousand times. In some imaginings she threw her arms around him. In others she struck him for leaving. Sometimes she demanded explanations. Sometimes neither of them spoke.

What she had never imagined was how young she would feel.

She touched his sleeve first. The cloth was damp. Then she gripped his arm hard enough to hurt.

“You’re real.”

“I think so.”

She embraced him. He smelled of salt and tar and the bitter tea he had always drunk. His arms closed around her, and she heard him make a broken sound.

“My little star,” he whispered.

“I’m not little.”

“No.” He stepped back and looked at her. Tears filled his eyes. “No, you’re not.”

“Where have you been?”

Elias glanced toward the window.

Outside, instead of Bellweather, dark water pressed against the glass. Pale shapes drifted in the depths.

“We should sit,” he said.

“I don’t want to sit.”

“The house prefers it.”

“The house?”

As if in answer, the walls creaked.

Elias lowered his voice. “This place listens.”

Mara remained standing. “Tell me.”

He rubbed a hand over his face. “The storm carried me beyond the reef. The mast broke. I went into the water. There was a light below me, so I swam toward it. I found a city on the ocean floor.”

“A city?”

“Not like ours. Older. Hungry in a way stone should not be hungry.” He looked at the ceiling. “It builds rooms from memories. Makes them comfortable. Gives you what you miss.”

Mara thought of the blue door standing alone in the mud.

“Why?”

“To keep us.”

“Us?”

Elias led her to the window.

At first she saw only dark water and drifting threads of weed. Then a light appeared in the distance, illuminating the shape of another house. Beyond it was another, and another—hundreds of windows glowing beneath the sea.

In one, an old woman brushed a little girl’s hair. In another, two soldiers played cards. A man danced alone in a ballroom while ghostly musicians moved their bows across silent violins.

“All taken by the sea?” Mara asked.

“Some drowned. Some opened doors, as you did. Some came willingly because they were promised the dead.”

“Are those people alive?”

“Some. Time is uncertain here.”

Mara turned from the window. “You could have come home today.”

“No.”

“The door opened.”

“Only for you.”

“How do you know?”

“Because it asked me what I wanted most.”

Cold traveled through Mara’s body.

“And you said my name.”

“Every day for eleven years.”

The kitchen lights flickered. A cupboard door eased open by itself.

Mara remembered the exposed seabed, the ocean waiting beyond the reef. “Why now?”

Elias looked afraid.

“Because the city is dying.”

A deep groan rolled through the house. The cups trembled.

“The city lives on longing,” he continued. “On the distance between what is and what we wish were true. It has fed on all of us, but it needs more. Today it opened every path it could.”

“To bring people in?”

“To bring Bellweather in.”

Mara ran to the door and pulled it open.

There was no beach beyond it now.

A street stretched through greenish darkness. Buildings leaned over a road paved with shells. Lamps glowed behind curtains. Doors of every color lined the walls, and through their open frames Mara glimpsed impossible places: a summer orchard, a nursery, a battlefield before the fighting, a ship sailing under bright stars.

People wandered the street.

Some wore Bellweather coats and carried lanterns. Mara recognized the baker, a pair of dockworkers, and Harbor Master Crenn’s youngest son. Each walked toward a different door with a look of wonder.

“They’re coming through,” Mara said.

“You must warn them.”

“How do I get back?”

Elias hesitated.

Mara understood.

“You don’t know.”

“There is a way. At the center of the city stands a tower. Inside is a bell made from the first anchor ever lost at sea. When it rings, all doors open.”

“Then we ring it.”

“The city will stop us.”

Mara looked at her father. “Have you tried?”

“At first. But this house showed me you at nine years old. Then ten. Then fifteen. I watched you grow. I knew it wasn’t real, but…” His gaze fell. “I became a coward.”

Mara wanted to deny it, but there was no time for comforting lies.

“Then be brave now,” she said.

They stepped into the street.

The city noticed them at once.

Lamps dimmed. Doors slammed. The road shifted beneath Mara’s boots, shells grinding like teeth. Far above, the unseen surface shimmered.

“This way,” Elias said.

They ran.

At the first crossing, a door opened directly in Mara’s path.

Her mother stood beyond it in a sunlit garden. She was laughing, dressed in a red gown Mara had never seen. Beside her stood Elias, young and unscarred. A nine-year-old Mara chased butterflies through the grass.

Her mother turned.

“Come in,” she called. “Everything is all right.”

Mara slowed.

She knew it was false. Yet the garden smelled of mint and summer rain. Her father’s laughter was exactly right. Even the sunlight felt warm on her face.

Elias seized her hand.

“Don’t look.”

Mara shut her eyes and let him pull her forward. The garden vanished behind a slamming door.

They passed more temptations. Elias saw a boat waiting on a calm sea, his long-dead brother waving from the deck. Mara saw herself as an old woman surrounded by children. They saw feasts, safe harbors, forgotten faces, and lives in which no one had ever left.

Each vision weakened when refused.

The city grew angry.

Walls bent inward. Water burst through windows and vanished before touching the ground. Voices called from drains and chimneys.

At last they reached a square.

The tower rose from its center, narrow and black, wrapped in chains. Its entrance had no door, only a dark opening.

Around it stood dozens of people.

Mara recognized villagers among strangers in ancient clothing. All stared into the tower entrance, where each apparently saw something different.

Tomas stood nearest. Tears ran into his beard.

“What do you see?” Mara asked.

“My wife,” he whispered. “She says she’s been waiting.”

Mara took his brass-hooked pole and struck him hard across the shin.

He yelped and spun toward her.

“Your wife,” Mara said, “would have told you to change that ridiculous hat.”

Tomas blinked. He looked at the tower, then back at Mara. Grief rearranged itself into anger.

“That she would.”

“Help me wake the others.”

While Tomas shouted and swung his pole, Mara and Elias entered the tower.

A spiral stairway descended rather than climbed. At the bottom waited a circular chamber. Its walls pulsed with faint blue light, and water dripped upward from the floor.

The bell hung over a bottomless pit.

It was green with age and large enough to shelter a cart. Black ropes bound its iron tongue. Across the pit stretched a bridge no wider than a plank.

Elias tested it with one boot.

The tower shook.

From the walls came the city’s voice, made from hundreds of whispers.

STAY.

The chamber disappeared.

Mara stood again in her childhood kitchen. Her mother kneaded bread at the table. Elias cleaned a fish by the sink. Rain tapped the window.

There had been no disappearance. No years of grief. No lonely Returning Days.

Her father glanced up. “Pass me the knife, little star.”

On the table lay the bone-handled knife he had carried to sea.

Mara picked it up.

Her hand was small again.

She wanted to stay so badly that wanting became a physical pain. Why should truth matter, if the lie was gentle? Why choose an empty chair, a tired mother, and eleven lost years?

Then she saw the calendar on the wall.

It showed the first Tuesday of November.

The day never changed here. Nothing changed. Nothing grew.

A life without loss was also a life without tomorrow.

Mara drove the knife into the table.

The kitchen cracked like glass.

She was back in the tower. The bridge pitched beneath her. Elias hung from its edge, gripping the plank with both hands.

Mara dropped flat and caught his wrist.

“Let me go,” he gasped. “Ring the bell.”

“No.”

“Mara—”

“I’ve done that already.”

She hauled until Tomas appeared behind her and grabbed Elias’s coat. Together they pulled him up.

Across the chamber, the bell waited.

They crawled over the bridge. At the bell, Mara cut the black ropes with the bone-handled knife. Elias and Tomas seized the iron tongue.

The city screamed.

Water poured down the stairway. The tower buckled. Faces emerged from the walls, mouths open in fury.

“Now!” Mara shouted.

They swung the iron tongue.

The first strike made no sound.

The second produced a note so deep Mara felt it in her bones.

On the third strike, the world opened.

Thousands of doors appeared in the air, in the walls, across the pit, and beneath the rising water. Through them shone beaches, ships, bedrooms, deserts, forests, and distant centuries.

“Go!” Elias yelled.

People flooded into the chamber. Some vanished through doors. Others froze, unable to recognize their own time.

Mara saw the blue door above the pit.

Beyond it lay Bellweather’s exposed seabed beneath a gray morning sky.

She pushed Tomas through. Then she turned to Elias.

He stood several paces away.

Water swirled around his waist. The city’s blue light shone through his body.

“No,” Mara said.

Elias looked down at his transparent hands.

“I told you I thought I was real.”

“You are.”

“Perhaps. But not in the way you need.”

The blue door began to close.

Mara reached for him. “Come with me.”

He stepped forward, but an invisible force held him. The house, the street, and the long years beneath the water had become part of him.

His face twisted with effort.

“I can’t.”

Mara grabbed his hand. It felt like cold rain.

The door narrowed.

Elias smiled, and in that smile she saw the father who had taught her knots, who had burned every breakfast, who had left and regretted leaving through an endless unmoving day.

“Tell your mother,” he began.

“You tell her.”

“Mara.”

“You tell her!”

The bell sounded again as the tower collapsed.

Elias pulled his hand free.

“You were worth every year,” he said.

Then he shoved her through the door.

Mara fell onto wet sand.

Tomas dragged her away as the blue door toppled. The moment it struck the ground, it became ordinary wood.

Across the seabed, doors burst open. People stumbled out: villagers, sailors, soldiers, merchants, and children dressed in the clothing of forgotten ages. Some dissolved into foam when touched by daylight. Others remained, blinking at the sky.

The ocean beyond the reef began to move.

A roar rose along the horizon.

“Run!” shouted Harbor Master Crenn.

Bellweather ran.

Mara and Tomas climbed through the harbor, helping an ancient sailor carry a wounded boy between them. Behind, the sea rushed back to claim the exposed land.

They reached the dunes as the first wave struck.

Boats lifted. Masts snapped. Returned treasures vanished beneath white water. The blue door spun once in the foam and was gone.

For three days, strangers wandered Bellweather. A woman from a kingdom no one remembered died peacefully in the chapel. Two brothers found that their family name still existed, though six hundred years had passed. A young sailor walked into a museum and discovered his own portrait.

Most of the returned faded before the week ended.

Mara searched among them for Elias.

She searched until there was no one left.

On the following morning, she sat with her mother at the kitchen table and told the whole story. Her mother listened without interrupting. When Mara repeated Elias’s final words, she covered her face.

Then she laughed.

It was not a happy laugh, but it was not entirely sorrowful either.

“That foolish man,” she said. “Always making someone else deliver his messages.”

Winter settled over Bellweather.

The sea stopped returning things.

On the first Tuesday of December, the villagers gathered at the beach out of habit. The tide behaved like any ordinary tide. Nothing lay on the sand but shells and weed.

The same happened in January, February, and March.

By spring, people stopped calling the day Returning Day. The harbor master removed the old warning signs. Children who had once searched for treasure began searching for crabs instead.

Mara continued to visit the beach before dawn.

She no longer expected her father. Expectation was another kind of door, and she had learned to be careful with doors.

Years later, when her mother’s hair had turned white and Tomas’s ridiculous hat had finally blown out to sea, Mara became keeper of the Bellweather lighthouse. She lived high above the reef and lit the lamp each evening for vessels crossing the dark.

During storms, sailors sometimes reported hearing a bell beneath the waves.

Mara heard it too.

But it did not call to her with promises. It did not show her gardens, kitchens, or lives without sorrow. It sounded distant and solemn, like a farewell repeated across great depths.

Once, on the first Tuesday of November, Mara found a wet boot standing upright outside the lighthouse door.

She sat beside it until sunrise.

Then she carried it inside, placed it near the stove, and went on with her day.
